Myths that sound scientific

"If they look up and to the right, they are lying"

An idea from neuro-linguistic programming that has failed every test.

In the 1970s, neuro-linguistic programming (NLP) claimed that the direction of someone's gaze reveals whether they are remembering or inventing: looking up to the right would mean constructing an image, in other words lying.

What the studies say

In 2012, Richard Wiseman and colleagues filmed people lying or telling the truth, and analysed real press conferences given by people appealing for help to find a missing relative, some of whom turned out to be guilty. Eye movements did not distinguish lies from truth.

In general there is no reliable bodily sign of lying, whether in the eyes or in touching the nose. People, including police officers and judges, do little better than chance when trying to spot lies from behaviour. Interviews that look for contradictions in the story work better.

References

  1. Wiseman, R. et al. (2012). The eyes don't have it: Lie detection and neuro-linguistic programming. PLoS ONE, 7(7), e40259.
  2. Bond, C. F. y DePaulo, B. M. (2006). Accuracy of deception judgments. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 10(3), 214–234.
